meeting_header: Date: 2025-02-18 | Time: 15:00-15:54 UTC | Duration: 54m | Attendees: Laura Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Astra Nova, Staff ML Eng), Tom Reynolds (Astra Nova, Platform), Marta Kovac (Astra Nova, SRE), Jamal Brooks (Astra Nova, Security)
transcript:
[00:00] Laura Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — I see Priya, Tom, Marta, Jamal — and me and Diego from Redwood. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya Nair: Doing good, thanks. We're excited — we want to make sure our observability plan works at token granularity without exploding cost.
[00:12] Diego Morales: Awesome. That's what we're focused on today — OTEL + token-level metrics, traces, dashboards, and how Redwood's runtime exports the telemetry.
[00:18] Tom Reynolds: Rough agenda for us: what signals are available, sampling strategies, how to hook into our existing OpenTelemetry pipeline, and any network/security implications for our VPC.
[00:24] Laura Kim: Yep, and performance tradeoffs — e.g., enabling token-level spans increases cardinality. We'll walk through patterns.
[00:30] Marta Kovac: Quick note: our retention and cost guardrails are strict. We can't ship unbounded high-cardinality metrics to backend.
[00:35] Diego Morales: Completely understood. We'll talk about aggregation and pre-aggregation at the Redwood side, plus export knobs.
[00:42] Jamal Brooks: And from security, KMS for any logs with PII, and TLS for trace export. We need to see SOC2 controls.
[00:48] Laura Kim: We'll share the security docs; Redwood supports OTLP over TLS and customer-managed keys for Private deployments.
[00:54] Priya Nair: Great. Can you start by describing what telemetry the runtime emits by default?
[00:58] Diego Morales: Sure. At a high level: request-level spans (inference request start/end), model-level metrics (latency p50/p95, token counts), batch-level events, and optional token-level spans. We emit OTLP/span batches, and we also have Prometheus-compatible metrics for aggregated counters/histograms.
[01:15] Priya Nair: When you say token-level spans — are those one span per token? That sounds massive.
[01:20] Diego Morales: It can be. The default token-level mode is "annotated-trace" where we write a parent span for the request and then append lightweight child events for token emit with a small set of attributes: token_index, token_len, generation_time_ms, and optionally logprobs. We avoid creating full heavyweight spans per token unless customers explicitly enable them.
[01:38] Tom Reynolds: So you do events versus spans by default — smart. How are token events exported in OTEL? OTLP? Are they metrics or logs?
[01:46] Diego Morales: They go in the trace stream as events inside the request span, so they piggyback on the request trace. That keeps cardinality lower because there's still one span id per request. We also synthesize derived metrics: tokens_generated_total (counter), token_latency_bucket (histogram) which are Prometheus-style and low-cardinality.
[02:01] Marta Kovac: If you include token text as an attribute, that's high-cardinality. Do you strip or hash token content?
[02:06] Diego Morales: We don't export raw tokens by default. Token text is redacted unless you enable debug mode. We recommend hashing with a salt if companies need content-level correlation.
[02:14] Priya Nair: Ok that helps. Our goal is to correlate latency spikes with specific patterns in prompts. We need some level of token context but not every token. Any batching recommendations?
[02:23] Diego Morales: Batching is twofold: runtime batching (multiple requests in GPU micro-batch) and batching at telemetry export. For runtime, we expose batch_size and max_latency_ms tunables. For telemetry, we buffer events and export every Xms or when buffer hits N events. You can tune the OTLP exporter batch_size and timeout.
[02:38] Tom Reynolds: Would batching telemetry delay critical alerts? If a tail latency incident is happening, we want near-real-time traces.
[02:44] Diego Morales: There's a tradeoff. We recommend reducing the telemetry batch timeout to 200-500ms for alerting hot paths. For cheaper longer-term analytics, use 5s aggregations. You can also use sampling where full events for error traces are always kept, while normal traces are sampled.
[02:58] Priya Nair: Sampling — is that head-based, tail-based? Any support for adaptive sampling tied to error rates?
[03:04] Diego Morales: We support both. On-host, we have head-based sampling settings (e.g., 1/10) and we provide integrations for tail-based sampling via your collector — e.g., set up a processor that retains traces with high latency or error flags. Redwood emits latency attributes so collector rules can be applied.
[03:18] Marta Kovac: Let's talk about aggregation and pre-aggregation. If token-level raw events are bad for our backend, can Redwood pre-aggregate on the agent?
[03:25] Diego Morales: Yes. For Dedicated and Private deployments we can enable pre-aggregation where the runtime computes token histograms and counts per request and exports only summaries. That mitigates both cardinality and bandwidth while preserving actionable SLO metrics.
[03:38] Laura Kim: To add, the hosted offering also supports aggregated export by default at higher retention tiers; if you need raw spans for debugging, we provide a toggle for a debug window.
[03:47] Jamal Brooks: About PII — if the prompt contains user data, how do you ensure it doesn't leak in telemetry?
[03:53] Diego Morales: We support configurable redaction rules: regex-based masking, and PII scrubbing pipelines pre-export. For Private deployments you can enforce zero-export policy where traces remain in the customer VPC and never flow to Redwood.
[04:06] Priya Nair: That zero-export option sounds useful. How does OTLP over VPC egress work? We're behind strict egress rules.
[04:12] Tom Reynolds: We'll need to confirm firewall ports.
[04:15] Diego Morales: For OTLP over gRPC/TLS we use port 4317 usually; you can also use OTLP/HTTP on 4318. When in Private mode we can peer the control plane and expose an endpoint internally or give you a collector container to run inside your VPC that forwards to your observability backend.
[04:30] Marta Kovac: Are there size/throughput considerations for the OTLP endpoint? If we stream token events for 50k reqs/sec that's heavy.
[04:36] Diego Morales: Absolutely. For high QPS, we advise: (1) aggregate on-host, (2) reduce token event frequency — e.g., sample 1 in N tokens, (3) use summary metrics (histograms) for latency rather than per-token numbers, and (4) enable compression and batched OTLP exports. We have performance numbers in the docs; I'll share a table.
[04:53] Laura Kim: Diego, maybe walk through an example trace payload and how you'd correlate to logs and metrics in Grafana.
[04:58] Diego Morales: Sure. Example: trace with trace_id=abc123, span request.start with attributes {model: "redwood-13b-quant", seq_len:512, batch_size:4}, events: [token_emit@0:{index:0, gen_ms:9}, token_emit@1:{index:1, gen_ms:11}...]. Those attributes let you filter traces in Jaeger/Tempo by model and seq_len. We also push derived metrics: request_latency_ms histogram labeled by model, route, and quantization_profile. In Grafana you can join the metrics (Prometheus) and traces (Tempo) using trace_id as a link in dashboards.
[05:23] Priya Nair: Do you recommend using Jaeger or Tempo? We run Grafana/Tempo stack internally.
[05:27] Diego Morales: Tempo is optimized for high-volume traces and integrates nicely with Grafana. We test with both Jaeger and Tempo — Tempo scales better for long retention and high-cardinality traces.
[05:36] Tom Reynolds: About quantization: does quantized execution change the telemetry attributes? I want to know when a request used int8 versus fp16 kernel.
[05:44] Diego Morales: Yes, we tag spans with quantization_profile and kernel_name. That way you can slice latency by kernel or quantization. It's important because int8 might lower throughput per core but change tail latency under certain sequences.
[05:56] Marta Kovac: On batching again — can we see per-batch metrics so we can tune batch size and latency SLOs?
[06:02] Diego Morales: Yes — batch_size_histogram and batch_fill_ratio gauges are emitted. You can create alerts for batch_fill_ratio dropping which indicates small batches (higher cost) or high batch latency.
[06:14] Priya Nair: For token-level quality monitoring — we also want to compute n-gram novelty and repetition metrics. Can those be computed at runtime and exported as metrics?
[06:22] Diego Morales: We have a plugin API — you can run a small post-processing hook per-request that computes aggregated quality metrics (e.g., repetition_count, avg_logprob) and export as low-cardinality metrics. The hook runs in a sandbox to avoid affecting model performance.
[06:36] Laura Kim: Note that those hooks are recommended for Dedicated/Private because they add CPU. Hosted can enable them for enterprise customers with a cost impact.
[06:44] Jamal Brooks: From a security/compliance point, we need auditability. Are all telemetry exports and versions logged?
[06:50] Diego Morales: Yes. There are audit logs for config changes, exporter toggles, and collector handshakes. For Private deployments we can forward audit logs into your SIEM.
[06:59] Tom Reynolds: Can you describe an example Grafana layout you recommend? We'll want panels for token throughput, p50/95 latency, batch fill, kernel utilization, and trace link columns.
[07:08] Diego Morales: Recommended dashboard: Top row — overall request throughput and error rate. Second — latency histograms by model/route. Third — token generation rate and token latency histogram. Fourth — batching metrics (batch size distribution), GPU utilization, and kernel stats. Fifth — trace sample table with clickable trace_id that opens Tempo. We'll send a JSON.
[07:27] Priya Nair: How do you avoid metric explosion across many routes and models?
[07:31] Diego Morales: Use labeling hygiene: keep cardinality-bounded labels (model, route, region, quant_profile) and avoid free-text labels. Also use relabeling rules in Prometheus to drop unnecessary labels. We can provide example relabel_configs.
[07:45] Marta Kovac: What's the impact on latency if we add the token event insertion into the span?
[07:50] Diego Morales: Minimal if you use events — we're appending an in-memory event struct; the heavy part is serialization and export. With batching the avg added per-token CPU is ~0.1-0.5ms depending on payload. If you create full spans per token it'll be bigger. We can run benchmarks on your workload.
[08:07] Priya Nair: Ok let's talk limits — is there a throttle or quota Redwood applies to telemetry exports on hosted?
[08:12] Laura Kim: Yes, hosted tiers have telemetry throughput quotas; Dedicated/Private give more control. We can provide numbers post-call — Diego will attach the table.
[08:20] Tom Reynolds: For our pilot, we want to capture full token events for a 2-hour window and then revert to aggregate exports. Is that feasible?
[08:27] Diego Morales: Feasible. We can enable a debug window via config flag per-namespace. For Hosted, debug windows are gated; for Private it's on your control. We'll coordinate retention since storing raw token traces for 2 hours at your QPS will be heavy.
[08:40] Priya Nair: There's also the data residency question. If raw traces must remain in EMEA, can we route telemetry to our EMEA Tempo?
[08:47] Diego Morales: Yes. You can configure the collector to forward to your in-region endpoint. For hosted, we can set the exporter endpoint to your Tempo host reachable via VPC peering.
[08:58] Jamal Brooks: A few specifics for our security review: we need mTLS support between Redwood runtime and our collector, and proof that logs are integrity checked.
[09:06] Diego Morales: We support mTLS for Private deployments and can provide cert rotation docs and integrity hashes for batched exports. We'll include the SOC2 excerpt.
[09:16] Priya Nair: What's the recommended sampling for production if we want to keep costs low but still monitor regressions?
[09:21] Diego Morales: A hybrid: 1% head-based sampling for general traces, plus rule-based retention for errors and latency > p99. Also stratified sampling by route: keep higher sampling for routes handling sensitive or revenue-critical flows.
[09:35] Tom Reynolds: Any built-in alerts Redwood provides?
[09:38] Laura Kim: We provide alert rule templates — e.g., p95 latency increase by >20% over baseline, token-generation-rate drop, batch fill < 0.3. These are easy to import into Grafana Alerting.
[09:49] Marta Kovac: Can we have token-level anomalies trigger a trace capture? For example, if repetition_count > 50 capture full token trace for 1k requests.
[09:57] Diego Morales: Yes, with an OTEL collector processor or with Redwood's adaptive sampler you can set a rule to retain full traces when a metric crosses a threshold.
[10:06] Priya Nair: Let's talk about instrumentation steps. What's the minimal config to get basic traces and metrics into our Grafana/Tempo stack?
[10:12] Diego Morales: Minimal path: run your OTEL collector (we'll share a compose snippet), configure an otlp_exporter to point to your Tempo, set resource attributes (service.name=astra-nova-inference), and enable request spans in the Redwood runtime config. Use Prometheus scrape for aggregated metrics. We'll give a one-page quickstart.
[10:29] Laura Kim: Diego, can you address the concerns about Cost vs. fidelity — maybe recommend a tracked pilot configuration?
[10:34] Diego Morales: For a pilot: enable request spans + token events sampled 1 in 100, export derived metrics at 30s intervals, enable debug window for two 1-hour sessions to capture full traces. Use pre-aggregation to keep storage in check. After pilot analyze storage/perf and tune.
[10:50] Tom Reynolds: That timeline works. We'll do pilot next week.
[10:53] Priya Nair: One more question — is there an SDK we can use in our app to enrich traces with business context (user_id hashed, feature_flag, request_id)?
[10:59] Diego Morales: Yes, we have an SDK snippet that sets trace attributes; we recommend hashing user_id and avoid raw PII. We'll share the SDK repo link.
[11:08] Marta Kovac: Regarding dashboards, please include an example panel that correlates GPU SM utilization with token latency.
[11:13] Diego Morales: Will do. We emit GPU metrics that your exporter collects; Grafana panel combining GPU SM% and token_latency_bucket is in the dashboard JSON.
[11:22] Jamal Brooks: For compliance, can we get proof of data deletion after the debug window?
[11:26] Laura Kim: Yes — Redwood can run a purge and provide a deletion report for Hosted customers or instructions for self-serve purge on Private.
[11:33] Priya Nair: Anything else?
[11:35] Laura Kim: Quick recap and next steps. We'll share: OTEL collector snippet, Grafana dashboard JSON, telemetry throughput table, security excerpts, and a pilot runbook. Diego will coordinate the benchmarks. Priya/Tom will run the pilot and upload traces. We'll reconvene after the pilot.
[11:49] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[11:52] Priya Nair: Thanks, bye.
[11:54] Laura Kim: Thanks all, ending call.
notes: Discussion leaned heavily into token events as OTEL 'events' to reduce cardinality.
Redwood recommended a hybrid sampling + pre-aggregation strategy for production.
Security: mTLS and zero-export policy addressed for Private deployments.
